strengths: Clear motivation and physical grounding: Introducing a gravity-aligned, absolute coordinate reference for camera control in text-to-video diffusion directly addresses a major limitation of prior relative-pose methods (e.g., CameraCtrl, AC3D), enabling consistent control over pitch and roll.

Clever data curation strategy: Leveraging 360-degree panoramic videos to synthesize camera paths across the viewing sphere effectively bypasses the severe bias towards eye-level, horizontal horizons present in standard video datasets.

Insightful solution to semantic-geometry entanglement: The 'null-pitch conditioning' strategy smartly decouples scene content semantics from viewpoint-induced visual content (e.g., sky vs. grass), preventing the diffusion model from ignoring camera guidance when prompts conflict with extreme viewpoints.

Strong experimental validation on extreme viewpoints: The paper demonstrates clear quantitative and qualitative advantages in PitchErr, GravityErr, and RotErr compared to relevant baselines when tested on challenging camera angles.
weaknesses: Limitations of the evaluation benchmark: The proposed SpatialVID-extreme benchmark contains only 140 videos, which is relatively small. Furthermore, roll angles in the benchmark are introduced via 2D image warping rather than true 3D camera rotation, which can introduce planar distortion artifacts not representative of real camera roll.

Limited translational control: The synthetic camera trajectory sampling focuses almost exclusively on rotational camera paths (pitch, roll, yaw), leaving explicit and disentangled camera translation control partially unaddressed, as acknowledged in the limitations.

Training scale and visual fidelity tradeoff: The model is trained on only 2,000 panoramic videos from WEB360, leading to a noticeable drop in aesthetic and video realism metrics (FID/FVD) compared to baselines trained on larger video datasets like RealEstate10K.

Baseline conditioning fairness: Providing AC3D with textual descriptions of absolute angles generated via template prompts is inherently out-of-distribution for a model trained solely on relative Plücker coordinates, which may slightly disadvantage the baseline comparison.

strengths: Addresses an important and often overlooked limitation in generative camera control: existing methods rely heavily on relative camera conditioning with respect to the first frame, which leaves global pitch, roll, and gravity orientation ambiguous.

The data generation strategy using geometrically calibrated 360-degree panoramic videos is well-motivated and effectively overcomes the strong horizontal/forward-facing viewpoint bias present in standard human-captured video datasets.

The proposed 'null-pitch conditioning' is an insightful solution to the semantic entanglement between prompt content and camera view direction (preventing the model from ignoring camera pitch when prompts mention ground-level or sky-level scene elements).
The paper is clearly structured, well-written, and supported by both qualitative visual comparisons and quantitative metrics showing substantial gains in absolute and relative orientation control.
weaknesses: The proposed SpatialVID-extreme evaluation benchmark is relatively small, comprising only 140 video clips, which limits the statistical robustness of the evaluation.

The benchmark introduces roll variation synthetically via planar 2D video warping rather than using authentic non-zero roll video captures or held-out panoramic projections, which may introduce unnatural image artifacts into the evaluation.
The camera trajectory sampling during training is restricted to rotational motion over existing SfM translation paths; free camera translation in 3D remains unaddressed in the generative formulation.

No perceptual user study is provided to assess visual realism, temporal consistency, and user satisfaction regarding trajectory adherence, which is standard practice in controllable generative video evaluation.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored challenge in controllable video generation: existing camera-conditioned text-to-video frameworks typically operate relative to an arbitrary first frame and suffer from the forward-facing bias of web video datasets, whereas this work grounds camera control in a physically meaningful, gravity-aligned coordinate frame.

The data sampling pipeline using 360° panoramic videos is practical and well-designed, allowing continuous and arbitrary sampling of pitch, roll, and FoV across the viewing sphere without requiring specialized sensor hardware.

The insight regarding prompt-viewpoint entanglement is valuable: standard captions from extreme angles describe only localized visual features (e.g., ground or sky), which conflicts with broader textual prompts during test time. The proposed 'null-pitch conditioning' effectively decouples camera angle from global scene semantics.

The construction of the SpatialVID-extreme evaluation benchmark fills a genuine evaluation gap by offering balanced distributions of pitch and roll to benchmark generative camera controllability under non-trivial angles.

Quantitative improvements in Table 1 on camera adherence (substantially reducing pitch error and gravity error compared to AC3D and PreciseCam + WAN) demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed orientation conditioning.
weaknesses: The camera trajectory generation pipeline is primarily focused on camera rotation; camera translations are tied to the original capture path of the 360° video. As noted in the discussion, the inability to freely synthesize 6-DoF trajectories with arbitrary translation remains a notable limitation.

Visual generation fidelity and realism metrics (FID and FVD) show a slight regression compared to some baselines (e.g., FID of 110.71 vs. 106.82 for AC3D, and FVD of 896.84 vs. 798.87 for PreciseCam + WAN). Visual artifacts are visible in challenging scenes (such as human crowds and background textures in Fig. 7).

Evaluation of absolute pitch and gravity error relies on Perspective Fields (a monocular camera calibration network). Because monocular estimators are themselves prone to higher estimation errors and ambiguity on extreme viewpoints (e.g., looking directly up or down), relying on them as ground truth judges could introduce measurement bias.

The benchmark generation for roll in SpatialVID-extreme relies on 2D image warping (-40° to +40°) rather than true 3D camera rotation, which can introduce synthetic boundary distortion and warp artifacts into the benchmark videos.

The model is trained on a relatively small set of 2,000 panoramic videos for only ~8,000 iterations, which likely restricts semantic diversity and domain coverage relative to models pre-trained on hundreds of thousands of standard video clips.

strengths: Addresses an important and recognized limitation in camera-controlled text-to-video generation: existing models suffer heavily from dataset bias towards upright, forward-facing cameras and struggle with extreme rotations (e.g., Dutch angles, looking straight up/down, full 360-degree rolls).

The data generation pipeline cleverly repurposes geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic video to synthetically extract perspective trajectories covering the full sphere, effectively eliminating human capture bias.

The proposed null-pitch conditioning provides an elegant and insightful solution to prompt-camera entanglement, preventing generative models from hallucinating ground semantics when the camera is instructed to look at the sky.

The paper introduces two thoughtful evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and a prompt-camera entanglement benchmark) specifically designed to diagnose camera-guidance failure modes under extreme orientations.

Demonstrates substantial quantitative improvements in absolute orientation accuracy (reducing PitchErr and GravityErr by substantial margins over baselines like UCPE and AC3D) while maintaining competitive generation quality.
weaknesses: Camera trajectory augmentation is restricted solely to rotations; camera translations are constrained by the physical motions present in the original panoramic videos, which may explain why translation error (TransErr) is slightly higher than some baselines (e.g., UCPE).

Model backbone disparities across baselines: the proposed method is built on WAN-2.2 5B, whereas some baselines use different architectures (e.g., AC3D uses CogVideoX-2B). While orientation error improvements stem from the conditioning framework, generation aesthetics (FID/FVD) could be influenced by backbone capability.

Heavy reliance on a cascade of pre-trained models (ViPE for relative motion, Perspective Fields for gravity estimation, and InternVL-3 for dense captioning), which introduces sensitivity to pose/gravity estimation noise and required manual filtering of training/benchmark data.

strengths: Clear motivation and problem formulation: The paper addresses a known and severe limitation in camera-controlled video synthesis, where existing methods struggle with large/extreme rotations (e.g., barrel rolls, top-down or looking straight up) due to biases in training datasets and relative camera representations.

Clever data curation and augmentation pipeline: Generating diverse perspective video trajectories on-the-fly from geometrically calibrated 360° panoramic videos effectively removes viewpoint bias while establishing a gravity-aligned world frame.

Insightful solution for prompt-camera entanglement: Identifying that captioning rotated crops leads to semantic entanglement (e.g., conditioning models to associate downward angles strictly with ground features) and proposing 'null-pitch conditioning' is a neat, principled, and effective design choice.

Thorough evaluation benchmarks: Introducing two dedicated test sets (SpatialVID-extreme and the PolyHaven entanglement benchmark) fills a gap in benchmarking extreme camera control in video generation.

Convincing quantitative and qualitative improvements: The method significantly outperforms existing baselines on absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr reduced to 9.35° compared to 16.25° for UCPE) and shows clear qualitative robustness under extreme motions (e.g., backflips, zenith views).
weaknesses: Camera translation control is relatively constrained: Because the trajectory sampling only modifies rotation while inheriting translations from the underlying SfM trajectories of 360° videos, translation error (TransErr) is somewhat higher than baselines like UCPE (0.72 vs. 0.44).

Backbone discrepancies across baselines: The proposed model builds upon WAN-2.2 5B, while baselines use different backbones (e.g., AC3D uses CogVideoX-2B, UCPE uses WAN-2.1). While orientation metrics reflect geometric adherence rather than just backbone capacity, some aesthetic differences (FID/FVD) may be affected by these differences.

Impact of 360° video quality: Real-world 360° equirectangular video datasets often suffer from stitching seams, blurred poles, and lower effective pixel density when cropped to perspective views. More discussion on how these camera-specific artifacts impact the diffusion training and final generation quality would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation in controllable text-to-video generation: existing methods are conditioned on camera poses relative to the initial frame and fail under extreme orientations (such as steep pitch, barrel rolls, and 360-degree rotations).

The data preparation pipeline is elegant: synthesizing perspective training sequences from 360-degree panoramic videos with gravity alignment provides comprehensive coverage of the SO(3) rotation space, overcoming the strong bias toward level horizons found in standard video datasets.

The insight regarding prompt-camera entanglement is clear and important. The proposed 'null-pitch conditioning' strategy (captioning upright forward-looking crops rather than rotated crops) effectively prevents semantic cues in the prompt from overriding geometric camera conditioning, which is verified by both qualitative and quantitative experiments.

The paper introduces two well-constructed evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and the PolyHaven entanglement benchmark) to rigorously evaluate extreme orientation adherence and disentanglement, which will benefit future research in camera-controllable video synthesis.

Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate substantial improvements in absolute orientation accuracy (PitchErr, GravityErr) and relative rotation consistency compared to relevant baselines like UCPE and AC3D.
weaknesses: Translation control remains constrained: as acknowledged in Section 5, the dynamic trajectory synthesis only randomizes camera rotations while reusing original SfM-estimated translations from the underlying 360 videos. As a result, the translation error (TransErr = 0.72) is higher than that of UCPE (0.44).

Relying on monocular estimators (Perspective Fields and VGGT) for ground-truth evaluation can be susceptible to failure modes in scenes with dynamic non-rigid objects, rapid motion blur, or ambiguous architectural cues, which could introduce measurement noise into the benchmark results.

While the look-down negative prompt strategy to mitigate selfie sticks/tripods is pragmatic, the paper could provide more quantitative details or ablation regarding how frequently these nadir artifacts still bleed into generated downward-looking shots.

strengths: Addresses an important and widely recognized limitation in camera-controlled video diffusion models: standard video datasets are heavily biased toward upright, forward-facing cameras with near-zero roll, causing existing models to fail on extreme rotations (e.g., top-down shots, Dutch angles, barrel rolls, and loops).

The data augmentation strategy using 360-degree panoramic videos, combined with SfM-based relative motion estimation and gravity alignment via Perspective Fields, effectively expands the camera trajectory distribution.

The proposed null-pitch conditioning is a neat and well-motivated solution to prompt-camera semantic entanglement, preventing the model from collapsing camera orientation to match semantic keywords in the text prompt (and vice versa).
The paper is method-agnostic, demonstrating successful integration across different backbones (CogVideoX, WAN-2.1, WAN-2.2) and conditioning representations (Plücker rays and UCPE).
The paper introduces two well-designed benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and an entanglement benchmark based on PolyHaven panoramas) with thorough quantitative and qualitative evaluations.
weaknesses: Camera trajectory augmentation on 360-degree videos is restricted to rotations; camera translations remain bound to the original capture path, which limits arbitrary 6-DoF trajectory synthesis.

The training corpus is relatively small (~4,800 filtered 360-degree video clips from PanoVid), which may constrain semantic and visual scene diversity compared to full-scale foundation video training.

Visual generation fidelity metrics (FID and FVD) show slight regression or stagnation compared to some image-to-video baselines, indicating that extreme angle generation can introduce geometric warping or visual artifacts (e.g., distorted structures in tall landmarks).

strengths: Addresses a fundamental limitation of existing camera-controlled video generation models: the lack of physical grounding (gravity alignment) and inability to faithfully handle extreme camera rotations (e.g., steep pitch, large roll, and full turnaround paths).

The data generation pipeline cleverly repurposes 360° equirectangular video datasets by combining SfM and single-image gravity estimation to extract arbitrary camera rotation trajectories across the full sphere.

Insightful identification and mitigation of the prompt-camera entanglement problem: using 'null-pitch conditioning' to generate video captions from forward-facing crops prevents the diffusion model from hallucinating prompt concepts that conflict with extreme camera angles (e.g., rendering ground when looking directly up).

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple foundational backbones (CogVideoX, WAN-2.1, WAN-2.2) and conditioning encodings (Plücker rays, UCPE), showing clear quantitative and qualitative advantages in pitch and gravity orientation errors over existing methods.
Introduction of two well-designed evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and PolyHaven prompt-camera entanglement) that will benefit the community.
weaknesses: The trajectory augmentation is restricted solely to rotations; camera translation still relies entirely on the pre-existing trajectories of the underlying panoramic video sequences.

The pipeline relies heavily on off-the-shelf estimators (ViPE for pose, Perspective Fields for gravity estimation, InternVL for captioning); systematic failure modes or biases in these upstream models (which required discarding 38% of the data) could propagate to the training distribution.
While orientation metrics show marked improvements, visual quality metrics (FID, FVD) and CLIP alignment scores show minor regressions or remain essentially flat compared to baselines.

Extreme viewing directions near the poles occasionally display visual distortions or blurriness, likely stemming from equirectangular projection stretching and tripod/rig artifacts inherent in 360° captures.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and prevalent limitation in video camera control: standard datasets (e.g., RealEstate10K) are heavily biased toward horizontal, forward-facing viewpoints, causing existing camera-controlled diffusion models to fail on extreme rotations (such as vertical pans, barrel rolls, and inverted views).

The gravity-grounded formulation combined with the 360-degree video sampling pipeline (Algorithm 1) provides a practical and scalable way to expose video diffusion models to the entire SO(3) rotational space without requiring manual capture of acrobatic camera paths.

The insight regarding prompt-camera entanglement is well-identified: generating text captions directly from pitched crops causes the model to associate camera angles with specific semantic content. The proposed 'null-pitch conditioning' effectively decouples global scene semantics from camera viewing angles.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple diffusion backbones (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1 1.3B, WAN-2.2 5B) and camera conditioning modalities (Plücker rays and UCPE), demonstrating that the pipeline is broadly applicable and yields substantial improvements in pitch and gravity orientation accuracy.

Introduction of two well-designed benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and the PolyHaven prompt-camera entanglement benchmark) to fill the absence of standardized evaluations for extreme camera motion in video synthesis.
weaknesses: The training pipeline samples arbitrary rotations on-the-fly, but camera translations remain constrained to the underlying physical motion of the source 360-degree videos, which may limit the diversity of coupled translational-rotational trajectories.

The SpatialVID-extreme benchmark synthesizes roll angles by planar image warping (between -40° and +40°), which can induce border distortion and resampling artifacts in the ground-truth reference videos used for FID/FVD computations.

The quantitative evaluation of absolute orientation relies heavily on monocular pose/gravity estimation networks (Perspective Fields and VGGT); while necessary in the absence of sensor ground truth, these estimators can suffer from elevated uncertainty under extreme viewpoints.

The negative prompt look-down conditioning strategy, while effective at suppressing tripod and selfie-stick artifacts, feels somewhat heuristic and points to a residual data hygiene challenge in 360-degree video datasets.
